F&B Knowledge Series

Guide to Premium Proteins

Nutritional value and culinary profiles of beef, mutton, veal, venison, chicken, duck, goose, squab and salmon.

By Nigel A. Thomas, Hospitality Executive · Updated October 2026

Walk into any serious kitchen and you will find that the menu is built on a handful of centre-of-the-plate proteins. Beef, mutton, veal, venison, chicken, duck, goose, squab and salmon each bring a distinct flavour, texture, nutritional profile and price point, and each demands its own handling. A chef who understands these nine proteins can build a menu that feels both generous and precise, while a service team that understands them can guide a guest to the right dish with confidence.

This guide expands on the infographic poster below and gives each protein a practical profile: what it offers nutritionally, how it behaves in the kitchen, which cuts and methods suit it, and how to present it. After more than thirty years in hospitality, on ships, in hotels and in restaurants across India, the Middle East and the USA, I have learned that the best menus are not the most complicated ones. They are the ones where every protein is chosen, cooked and served for a reason. If you are also working on the wider nutrition picture, the Top 20 Protein-Rich Foods guide is a useful companion.

What Makes a Protein “Premium”?

“Premium” is not a scientific term, and it does not simply mean expensive. In professional kitchens a protein earns the label through a combination of qualities: the care taken in rearing or catching it, the consistency of the cut, its flavour and texture when cooked properly, its nutritional density, and its ability to carry a dish on its own. A well-sourced chicken breast can be a premium product, while a poorly handled cut of beef is not, whatever the price on the invoice.

Five factors usually decide where a protein sits on the quality scale:

  • Provenance and rearing: breed, diet, age at slaughter or harvest, and welfare standards all shape taste and texture.
  • Cut and grade: the muscle used, the amount of marbling, and the trim determine how the meat eats.
  • Handling: chilling, ageing, hanging and cold-chain control protect quality between farm and plate.
  • Nutritional density: a good balance of protein, vitamins and minerals for the calories delivered.
  • Culinary versatility: how many dishes and techniques the protein can support.

Protein Basics Every Chef Should Know

Meat, poultry and fish are all sources of complete protein, meaning they supply all of the essential amino acids the body cannot make for itself. Beyond protein, each brings a different set of nutrients, and understanding them helps you explain a dish honestly to guests who ask about it.

  • Iron: red meats such as beef, mutton and venison are rich in heme iron, which the body absorbs more readily than the iron found in plant foods.
  • B-vitamins: B12, B6 and niacin are abundant in meat and fish and support energy metabolism and the nervous system.
  • Zinc and selenium: important for immunity and found in good amounts in red meat, poultry and fish.
  • Omega-3 fatty acids: found mainly in oily fish such as salmon, and in smaller amounts in grass-fed meat.
  • Fat quality: the amount and type of fat differ widely. Venison and chicken breast are very lean, while duck and goose carry a lot of fat, much of it unsaturated.

A note on numbers: nutrient values vary with breed, feed, cut, trimming and cooking method, and published figures differ between food composition tables. Treat any figure you quote to guests as approximate and rely on your supplier specification or your national food composition database when accuracy matters, for example on allergen and nutrition labelling.

Beef: High in Iron and B-Vitamins

Beef is the benchmark protein of the Western menu. It is rich in heme iron, zinc and vitamin B12, and a lean cooked portion delivers roughly 26 to 27 g of protein per 100 g. Flavour comes from muscle structure and fat: tender cuts such as fillet and striploin cook quickly, while working muscles such as shin, brisket and chuck have more connective tissue and reward long, slow cooking.

Marbling, the fine streaks of intramuscular fat, is what makes a ribeye juicy and flavourful, and it is the reason premium grading systems reward it. Dry-ageing concentrates flavour and tenderises the meat by allowing natural enzymes to work, but it also costs yield through moisture loss and trim, which you must reflect in your menu pricing.

Kitchen notes: season steaks generously, rest them after cooking so the juices redistribute, and match the cut to the method. Grill or pan-sear tender cuts, braise tough ones. Beef pairs naturally with structured red wines, as our food and wine pairing guide explains. In India, rules on beef vary by state and by community, so check local regulations and your guests’ expectations before featuring it.

Mutton: Rich in Zinc and Omega-3

Mutton is traditionally the meat of mature sheep, with a deeper, more assertive flavour than lamb. The poster shows a rack of lamb chops, which is the young, tender end of the sheep family. Terminology is a trap here, so be precise on your menu: lamb comes from a sheep under about a year old, hogget from a sheep between lamb and mutton, and mutton from an adult. In India, “mutton” on a menu very often means goat meat, so guests may arrive with a different expectation from the one the word carries in the West.

Nutritionally, sheep meat is a good source of zinc, iron and B12, and meat from grass-fed animals tends to contain more omega-3 fatty acids than grain-fed meat, although the amounts are modest compared with oily fish. Its fat has a distinctive flavour that some guests love and others avoid, so trimming and cooking choices matter.

Kitchen notes: racks and cutlets suit quick, high-heat cooking and are usually served pink. Shoulder, shank and neck are ideal for slow braises, curries and biryani, where the longer cooking breaks down connective tissue and the stronger flavour stands up to spices. Rosemary, garlic, mint and cumin are classic partners.

Veal: Lean and Easy to Digest

Veal comes from young calves and is prized for its pale colour, fine grain and delicate flavour. It is lean, with little marbling, and its fine muscle fibres give a tender bite, which is why it is often described as light and easy to eat. Its mildness makes it a perfect carrier for sauces, herbs and crumb coatings.

Because veal is so lean, it dries out easily and punishes overcooking. Cutlets and escalopes are typically pounded thin and cooked very quickly, as in Milanese or schnitzel preparations. Larger cuts such as the loin can be roasted gently and served medium. Osso buco, the cross-cut shank braised until it falls from the bone, shows the opposite end of the veal spectrum, rich in gelatine and deeply savoury.

Kitchen notes: use moderate heat, add moisture through sauces or butter, and rest the meat well. Welfare and rearing standards vary considerably between producers, so source from suppliers you trust and know how to explain their practices to guests who ask.

Venison: Ultra-Lean Protein

Venison is the meat of deer and is among the leanest red meats available, with very little fat and a high protein content. It is rich in iron and B-vitamins and has a deep, slightly sweet, mineral flavour. Farmed venison is milder and more consistent than wild, and it is the form most professional kitchens use.

The lack of fat is both venison’s strength and its challenge. It cooks quickly, dries out if taken past medium, and benefits from added fat in the form of a butter baste, bacon, a rich sauce or a marinade. Tender loin and saddle cuts suit searing and are best served pink, while shoulder and haunch suit stewing and braising.

Kitchen notes: juniper, red wine, redcurrant, berries, beetroot and earthy mushrooms all complement its flavour. Sourcing deserves special attention. Hunting of wild deer is restricted in India under wildlife protection law, so venison served in hospitality is generally farmed and often imported. Always buy from licensed suppliers with full traceability.

Chicken: High Protein, Low Fat

Chicken is the world’s most widely eaten meat and the workhorse of almost every menu. A cooked, skinless breast delivers around 31 g of protein per 100 g with very little fat, which is why it features so heavily on healthy and fitness-oriented menus. The leg and thigh carry more fat and more flavour, and they stay juicy through longer cooking.

Its mild taste makes chicken one of the most adaptable proteins in the kitchen: it takes on the character of marinades, spices, sauces and smoke with ease. The same bird can become a roasted supreme, a tandoori tikka, a fried cutlet, a poached salad or a rich curry.

Kitchen notes: chicken must be cooked through, and its safe internal temperature is 74°C (165°F). Overcooked breast turns dry and stringy, so brining, marinating or cooking on the bone helps. Chicken is also the protein most often linked with cross-contamination, so strict separation of raw and cooked product, dedicated boards and thorough handwashing are essential.

Duck: Healthy Fats and Minerals

Duck is a richer, darker and more flavourful poultry than chicken. Although it is a bird, the breast is treated much like a red meat, and the layer of fat under the skin is the source of its character. Duck provides iron, selenium and B-vitamins, and much of its fat is unsaturated, which makes duck fat prized for roasting potatoes and confit.

The skin on a duck breast is the key to success. Scoring it in a crosshatch, as shown on the poster, lets the fat render out slowly in a cold pan, leaving the skin thin and crisp while the meat stays tender. Legs are best cured and cooked slowly in their own fat as confit, or braised.

Kitchen notes: many restaurants serve duck breast pink, but this is a food safety decision that must follow your HACCP plan and local regulations, since poultry guidance generally calls for a higher core temperature. Fruit sauces such as orange, cherry and plum, along with spices like star anise and five-spice, balance its richness. Pinot Noir is a classic wine partner.

Goose: Rich in Healthy Unsaturated Fats

Goose is the traditional centrepiece of festive tables across Europe. It has a large frame, a thick layer of fat and dark, rich meat. Goose fat is high in unsaturated fats compared with many animal fats, which, together with its flavour, has made it a prized cooking medium for roasting and confit.

The poster shows a goose breast, a cut that is lean in the meat itself and can be cooked in a similar way to duck breast: skin scored and rendered, then rested. A whole roast goose is a different proposition. It needs time, careful rendering of fat during the roast, and often a pricking of the skin to release it.

Kitchen notes: save the rendered fat, which is a valuable kitchen ingredient. Sweet and sharp accompaniments cut through the richness, so think of apples, prunes, red cabbage and chestnuts. Goose is a seasonal and specialist item, so plan your purchasing and be honest with guests about availability.

Squab: Nutrient-Dense and Tender

Squab is a young domesticated pigeon, harvested while still tender, usually before it has fully matured. Its meat is dark, fine-grained and richly flavoured, often compared to a cross between chicken and game. It is a good source of iron and protein in a small, elegant portion, which is why it appears on fine-dining and tasting menus.

A single bird is small and is commonly served as one portion or split between two. The breast is the prized part and is often served pink, while the legs may be braised or confit. Because it is so lean, squab can dry out quickly, so careful, quick cooking and resting are important.

Kitchen notes: roasting on the crown, pan-roasting the breast and making a jus from the carcass all work well. Spices such as cinnamon and cumin, along with figs, dates and pomegranate, suit its dark, slightly gamey flavour. As with duck, serving it pink requires a documented food safety approach.

Salmon: Omega-3 Fatty Acids

Salmon is the premium fish of the group and the only protein here that is a significant source of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids, namely EPA and DHA. Depending on species and whether it is farmed or wild, a 100 g portion can supply roughly one to two and a half grams of these fats, which are associated with heart and brain health. It also provides high-quality protein, vitamin D and B12.

Salmon’s fat content makes it forgiving and versatile. It can be grilled, pan-seared, roasted, poached, smoked, cured as gravlax or served raw in sushi and sashimi. The flesh flakes along its natural seams, and the skin crisps beautifully when cooked on a hot pan with a little patience.

Kitchen notes: the biggest risk with salmon is overcooking, which dries it and drives the white albumin to the surface. Cook it until it is just opaque with a slightly translucent centre if your food safety plan allows, or to a higher temperature if it does not. Fish is a major allergen, so label dishes clearly. Lemon, dill, capers, mustard and crisp white wines suit it well, and our seafood varieties guide covers the wider fish and shellfish range.

Cooking and Doneness Guide

The table below compares the doneness many chefs prefer for each protein with the standard food safety reference temperature. Serving below the reference temperature is a risk-based decision that depends on the quality and source of the product, your HACCP plan, the guest’s informed choice and the regulations that apply in your venue. When in doubt, cook to the reference temperature and use a calibrated probe thermometer.

ProteinTypical chef preferenceSafety reference (core)
Beef steakMedium-rare, 54 to 57°C63°C with a 3-minute rest
Mutton / lamb rackPink, 54 to 60°C63°C with a 3-minute rest
Veal loinMedium, 57 to 60°C63°C with a 3-minute rest
Venison loinMedium-rare, 52 to 57°C63°C for whole cuts
ChickenCooked through74°C
Duck / goose breastPink, 54 to 60°C (risk-managed)74°C for poultry
Squab breastPink, 55 to 60°C (risk-managed)74°C for poultry
SalmonMedium-rare, 50 to 52°C63°C

Ground and minced products, such as burger patties made from beef or lamb, should be cooked to 71°C because bacteria on the surface are mixed through the meat during grinding. Always rest meat after cooking and probe the thickest part, away from bone.

Sourcing, Storage and Food Safety

Quality starts before the kitchen. Buy from approved suppliers who can show certification, traceability and a clean cold chain. On delivery, check the temperature and appearance: chilled meat and poultry should arrive at 5°C or below, and fish should be on ice with clear eyes, bright gills and a fresh, clean smell. Reject anything outside your specification.

  • Separate and store by risk: keep ready-to-eat food above raw products, and store raw poultry on the lowest shelf so it cannot drip onto other food.
  • Keep it cold: hold chilled product at 5°C or below, and frozen product at minus 18°C or below.
  • Label and rotate: date everything and follow first in, first out, so older stock is used first.
  • Thaw safely: thaw under refrigeration or in controlled conditions, never at room temperature.
  • Prevent cross-contamination: use colour-coded boards and knives, clean as you go and wash hands between tasks.
  • Respect allergens: fish is a major allergen and must be declared and handled with care.

Costing, Yield and Portioning

Premium proteins are expensive, so the difference between a profitable menu and a loss-making one often lies in yield control. The price you pay per kilogram is not the price you pay per portion. Bones, fat, trim, skin and cooking loss all reduce what ends up on the plate, so every protein should have a documented yield test.

  • Butchery yield: weigh the item as purchased, then weigh the usable trimmed portion. The ratio gives the real cost of the usable product.
  • Cooking loss: weigh before and after cooking to find the shrinkage, which is higher in dry-aged beef, roast goose and slow-cooked cuts.
  • Standard portions: define the portion weight in the recipe, for example a steak or fillet portion for a main course, and train the team to cut to it.
  • Use the trim: bones become stock and jus, fat becomes cooking medium, and trim can go into mince, sausages or staff meals, which lowers real food cost.
  • Price for value: review the margin on each protein regularly and adjust the menu when supplier prices move.

Matching Proteins With Wine

Wine can lift a protein dish or flatten it. In broad terms, structured reds such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah suit beef, mutton and venison, while lighter, fruitier reds such as Pinot Noir suit duck, squab and veal. Chicken is flexible and can take a rich Chardonnay or a light red. Salmon works with Pinot Noir as well as with crisp whites and sparkling wine. For the reasoning behind each match, read our full guide to food and wine pairing.

Menu Writing and Service

How a protein is described affects how guests order it. Be specific and honest, and train staff to explain each dish in simple language.

  • Name the cut and the cooking method, for example “pan-roasted duck breast with orange jus”, rather than using vague words.
  • State the origin or style when it adds value, and avoid claims you cannot support.
  • Use clear terms for mutton, lamb and goat so that guests know what they are ordering.
  • Ask guests how they like their steak or duck, explain your doneness policy, and give consumer advice where required.
  • Flag allergens, especially fish, and any items cooked pink.
  • Offer a lighter option, such as chicken or salmon, and a rich option, such as duck or beef, so every guest finds a fit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which of these proteins is the leanest?

Venison and skinless chicken breast are the leanest options, followed by veal. Duck and goose are the richest in fat, although much of that fat sits in the skin and can be rendered away.

Is red meat unhealthy?

Red meat provides valuable iron, zinc and B12, and it can be part of a balanced diet. Health authorities generally advise moderating portions and the frequency of processed and heavily charred meat. Lean cuts, sensible portions and varied proteins are a sound approach.

Why is mutton cooked longer than lamb?

Mutton comes from older animals and has more developed muscle and connective tissue, so it needs slow, moist cooking to become tender. Lamb is younger and tender enough for quick, high-heat cooking.

Can I serve duck or salmon rare?

That is a decision for each venue. It depends on supplier quality, your HACCP plan, local regulations and informed guest choice. If you cannot meet those conditions, cook to the safe reference temperature.

How do I keep lean proteins from drying out?

Do not overcook them. Use a probe thermometer, add fat through a baste or sauce, brine or marinate where suitable, and always rest the meat before serving.

Final Thoughts

Beef, mutton, veal, venison, chicken, duck, goose, squab and salmon are nine very different ingredients, and treating them as interchangeable “mains” is the quickest way to waste their potential. Each has its own nutrition, flavour, texture, risk profile and cost, and the skill of a professional kitchen lies in respecting those differences: choosing the right cut, cooking it to the right point, and presenting it honestly.

Use the poster as a quick reference on the pass or in the training room, and the guide above as the reasoning behind it. Taste widely, keep your yield records, protect your cold chain, and always explain your dishes in plain language.
